summary: Specifies how to use several elliptic curve cryptography Brainpool curves for authentication and key exchange in TLS. It gives implementers a way to use these curves where they are required or preferred.

plainLanguage.summary: Brainpool curves are an alternative set of elliptic curves for cryptography. TLS picked the curve for a session with a number from a registry, and no numbers existed for the Brainpool curves. This RFC assigns three of them and records them with IANA.

questions: how to use brainpool for key exchange
subtitle: How to offer the Brainpool elliptic curves in TLS for authentication and key exchange.

tldr.problem: TLS negotiates the elliptic curve used for key exchange with a number from a registry. The Brainpool curves had no such numbers, so a TLS implementation could not offer them even though certificates could already carry them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds three NamedCurve types, 26, 27 and 28, for brainpoolP256r1, brainpoolP384r1 and brainpoolP512r1, and IANA has recorded them in the EC Named Curve registry of the TLS Parameters registry, with the DTLS-OK flag set for all three.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that updates RFC 4492, the document defining the elliptic curve cipher suites for TLS. Implementations that need or prefer the Brainpool curves now have registered values to negotiate, and the RFC adds the usual advice on key sizes and side-channel resistance.

facts.label: Usable with
facts.value: TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, TLS 1.2 and Datagram TLS

today: RFC 7027 is an Informational RFC published in October 2013. It updates RFC 4492, which defines the elliptic curve cipher suites for TLS, by adding the Brainpool NamedCurve values, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Brainpool Curves and TLS
sections.content:
RFC 5639 specified a new set of elliptic curve groups over finite prime fields for use in cryptographic applications. They are denoted as ECC Brainpool curves, they were generated in a verifiably pseudo-random way, and they comply with the security requirements of the relevant standards from ISO, ANSI, NIST and the Standards for Efficient Cryptography Group.

RFC 4492 defines the use of elliptic curves for authentication and key agreement in TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1, and those mechanisms may also be used with TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246). The ASN.1 object identifiers defined in RFC 5639 already allow the Brainpool curves to be used in TLS, for client or server authentication, by reference in X.509 certificates according to RFC 3279 and RFC 5480.

What was missing was key exchange. A handshake chooses the elliptic curve group with a number taken from a registry, and no such numbers existed for the Brainpool curves. This document specifies those values for three curves from RFC 5639.
sections.plainLanguage: A TLS session picks its curve with a number from a registry. Certificates could already name a Brainpool curve, but the handshake could not. This RFC supplies the missing numbers.

sections.title: The Brainpool NamedCurve Types
sections.content:
According to RFC 4492, the name space NamedCurve is used for negotiating elliptic curve groups for key exchange during a handshake that starts a new TLS session. This document adds new NamedCurve types for three elliptic curves defined in RFC 5639, in the following enumeration.

Three sizes are covered: a 256-bit curve, a 384-bit curve and a 512-bit curve, assigned the values 26, 27 and 28. The RFC also notes that these curves are suitable for use with Datagram TLS (RFC 6347), the datagram version of TLS.

Test vectors for a Diffie-Hellman key exchange using each of these curves are given in Appendix A of the RFC, with the same notation used for the Brainpool test vectors in RFC 6954.
sections.plainLanguage: Three Brainpool curves get registry values: 26 for the 256-bit curve, 27 for the 384-bit curve and 28 for the 512-bit curve. The RFC also says they work with Datagram TLS.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA has assigned numbers for the three curves in the EC Named Curve registry of the Transport Layer Security Parameters registry. Each entry records its value, the curve name, a DTLS-OK flag and the reference to this RFC. The DTLS-OK column reads Y for all three, which matches the statement in Section 2 that the curves are suitable for Datagram TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The three values are now in the IANA registry that TLS implementations read to agree on a curve. All three are marked as usable with Datagram TLS.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5246 apply to the Brainpool curves described in this document. The confidentiality, authenticity and integrity of the TLS communication are limited by the weakest cryptographic primitive applied, so to reach a maximum security level when using one of the curves for authentication and or key exchange in TLS, the key derivation function, the algorithms and key lengths of symmetric encryption, and message authentication, along with the algorithm, bit length and hash function used for signature generation, should be chosen according to the recommendations of NIST Special Publication 800-57 and RFC 5639. The private Diffie-Hellman keys should be selected with the same bit length as the order of the group generated by the base point G and with approximately maximum entropy.

Implementations of elliptic curve cryptography for TLS may be susceptible to side-channel attacks, where an attacker learns secrets from how the computation behaves. Particular care should be taken by implementations that internally transform curve points to points on the corresponding twisted curve, using the map (x',y') = (x*Z^2, y*Z^3) with the coefficient Z specified for that curve in RFC 5639, in order to take advantage of the efficient arithmetic the twisted curve's special parameters allow. The twisted curve itself offers the same level of security as the corresponding random curve, through mathematical equivalence, but arithmetic based on small curve parameters may be harder to protect against side-channel attacks. The RFC points to the BSI minimum requirements and to the Guide to Elliptic Curve Cryptography for general guidance on resisting such attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual TLS security rules apply. The RFC also warns that an implementation using the twisted curves for faster arithmetic has to protect that arithmetic against timing attacks.

sections.title: Test Vectors in Appendix A
sections.content:
Appendix A of the RFC gives test vectors for example Diffie-Hellman key exchanges using each of the three curves, so that implementations can check that they agree with each other.

The notation names the secret key of party A as d_A, the x and y coordinates of the public key of party A as x_qA and y_qA, the same four values for party B, and the coordinates of the shared secret as x_Z and y_Z. The x coordinate of the shared secret is the hex representation of the pre-master secret. The field elements are written as hexadecimal values using the FieldElement-to-OctetString conversion method specified in SEC 1.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix lists worked examples for each curve so that two implementations can check they compute the same shared secret.
